background.definition: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of the ascitic fluid in the absence of a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source of infection.Peritonitis is diagnosed if there is a surgically treatable source of intra-abdominal infection.

list.listitem: SBP is seen in 8% to 27% of hospitalized patients who have cirrhosis and ascites.
SBP carries an in-hospital mortality rate of 20% to 40%.
Recurrence occurs in 70% of patients who survive at 1 year.
Infection is usually monomicrobial. Polymicrobial infection should raise suspicion for secondary bacterial peritonitis.

Sixty percent of cases are due to Gram negative bacteria (Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are most common). One-quarter of the cases are due to Gram positive organisms, with Strep species being most commonly cultured.
Proton pump inhibitor use is associated with SBP in patients with cirrhosis (OR = 2.7).
Infection is thought to occur due to translocation of bacteria across the mucosa of the gut wall.

Cirrhotic patients often have bacterial overgrowth of the small intestine, leading to more bacterial penetration of mucosal defenses. These patients have ineffective chemotaxis and clearing of bacteria, allowing bacteria to seed lymph structures and enter the bloodstream.
Prolonged bacteremia leads to infection of the ascitic fluid.
A baseline MELD (Model for End-stage Liver Disease) score can predict the first episode of SBP in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

Patients undergoing serial large-volume outpatient paracentesis should have a screening cell count and differential performed on the ascitic fluid. Cultures should not be obtained routinely in the asymptomatic outpatient. C
Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated in cirrhotic patients with acute GI bleeding. Their use decreases mortality by 29% and decreases bacterial infections by 58%. B
Primary prophylaxis with antibiotics is also justified in patients with cirrhosis and ascites with ascitic protein <1 g/dL or with serum bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL. B
Patients with a previous episode of SBP should receive long-term antibiotic prophylaxis with daily norfloxacin 400 mg daily or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole one DS tablet 5 days per week. B
Evidence for antibiotic prophylaxis is very low certainty and evidence does not clearly identify a benefit and does not indicated which antibiotic is most beneficial.
A meta-analysis of observational studies showed that in patients with cirrhosis, the use of proton pump inhibitors increases the risk of SBP.C
Suspect SBP in any patient with chronic liver disease and fever or abdominal pain. C

Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear leukocyte (PMN) count >250/mm3 is the standard for diagnosis. This should prompt antibiotic therapy regardless of culture positivity. Obtain cultures at the bedside for all patients. B
Bedside use of reagent strips is very specific but lacks sensitivity to replace standard fluid testing. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Abdominal rigidity, polymicrobial, ascitic fluid parameters (LDH > upper limit of serum LDH, glucose <50 mg/dL, total protein >1 g/dL)

list.listitem: SBP should be suspected in any patient with chronic liver disease who presents with fever or abdominal pain.
The most common presenting symptoms are nonspecific and include fever (69%), abdominal pain (59%), hepatic encephalopathy (54%), diarrhea (32%), ileus (30%), and shock (21%); 10% are asymptomatic.

On physical examination patients may have tenderness and pain, but rigidity is usually lacking due to the layer of ascitic fluid between the visceral and parietal membranes. The presence of rigidity suggests secondary peritonitis or an alternate diagnosis.
See chapter on diagnosis of abdominal pain for more on the general evaluation of patients with abdominal pain.

Paracentesis should be performed urgently and ascitic fluid sent for cell count and differential. Diagnosis is made by an ascitic fluid PMN count >250/mm3. Clear ascitic fluid makes SBP much less likely but does not completely rule it out.

A systematic review found that the best tests to rule in SBP in patients with ascites were >1000 WBCs/mcl in the ascitic fluid (LR+ 9.1) and >500 polymorphonuclear cells/mcl in the ascitic fluid, and ascitic fluid pH <7.35 (LR+ 9.0). Findings that best ruled out SBP were <500 PMNs/mcl (LR− 0.16) and <500 WBCs/mcl (LR− 0.21).

Bedside use of leukocyte esterase test strips (Multistix) allows for immediate diagnosis at the bedside and rapid initiation of treatment. The strips are very specific and helpful when positive but lack the sensitivity to rule out infection when negative and should not replace standard ascitic fluid analysis.

Cultures should be obtained by inoculating ascitic fluid directly into blood culture bottles at the bedside. Bedside inoculation versus laboratory inoculation increases culture positivity from 50% to 80%.

Ascitic fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), total protein, and glucose should be done if secondary peritonitis is suspected. LDH and protein are higher in secondary peritonitis, while glucose is lower. See “Differential Diagnosis.”
Multiple organisms, ascites fluid LDH ≥ serum LDH, ascitic fluid glucose <50 mg/dL, or ascitic fluid total protein >1 g/dL are red flags for secondary peritonitis.
SBP should be suspected in any patient with chronic liver disease who presents with fever or abdominal pain.
The classification of ascitic infections is shown in . See chapter on diagnosis of abdominal pain for a broader differential diagnosis of abdominal pain.
Paracentesis should be performed urgently and ascitic fluid sent for cell count and differential.
Broad spectrum empiric antibiotics should be started as soon as SPB; a third-generation cephalosporin is most frequently recommended. B
An oral regimen with a fluoroquinolone (eg, cirpofloxacin) is a reasonable alternative if there is no organ dysfunction or systemic symptoms of infection; data from RCTs is lacking. B
IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 decreased mortality and renal failure in one study of high-risk patients. B
Avoid all nephrotoxic agents (eg, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast dye). B

Broad spectrum antibiotics should be started empirically. A Cochrane review did not find superiority of any specific regimen, but third-generation cephalosporins (typically cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours) have been extensively studied and achieved cure in 85% of patients.The Cochrane review concluded that 5 days of treatment was equivalent to 10 days of treatment.
When guided by therapeutic response, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, and ciprofloxacin are equally efficacious for the treatment of SBP in cirrhosis with ascites.
Patients with culture negative neutrocytic ascites (≥250 PMN per mm3) have similar mortality as those with positive cultures and should therefore receive full treatment with empiric antibiotics.

IV albumin 1.5 g/kg of body weight within 6 hours of diagnosis followed by a second dose of 1 g/kg of body weight on day 3 decreased mortality from 29% to 10% and renal failure from 33% to 10% in a single study of high risk patients. Current treatment guidelines recommend albumin for SBP.A meta-analysis of 4 small studies (total of 288 high-risk patients) demonstrates a mortality rate of 35% without albumin vs. 16% with albumin (NNT = 5).

Several regimens with oral antibiotics (eg, ofloxacin 400 mg bid) in patients without shock, encephalopathy, or bleeding have been studied and are recommended by guidelines for selected patients.Although the studies found similar cure rates and mortality rates, a Cochrane review concluded that these studies were too small to be conclusive.

Repeat paracentesis can be performed at 48 hours after initiation of antibiotics to document at least a 25% decrease in the number of neutrophils, which correlates with the treatment response. Repeat paracentesis should be done if there is a lack of response to the initial antibiotic treatment, but this is not recommended routinely.
Nephrotoxic agents should be avoided to prevent a hepatorenal syndrome.
Liver transplantation should be considered for all patients who survive SBP as it portends advanced liver disease and mortality.
In-hospital mortality remains 20% to 40% despite clearing of infection, largely due to progressive liver failure, renal failure, and bleeding. B

Although bacterial clearance is achieved with antibiotics, mortality after an episode of SBP remains high (1 and 2 year survival of 30% and 20%, respectively). This is due to worsening liver failure, renal failure, and GI hemorrhage. B

Bacterial infection-induced renal failure occurs in one-third of patients and increases mortality from 7% to 42%; it is predicted by MELD score, peak WBC count, and nonresolution of infection. Type I hepatorenal syndrome is the most concerning form of renal failure due to its progressive nature. B
